metadata.note: Three connected companies that together built the Hoosick Valley route east from Troy, filling a gap in this dataset: before this file nothing came within 20 km of Hoosick Junction, Hoosick Falls or Bennington. The Troy & Boston ran 35 miles from Troy up the Hoosic River to the Vermont state line; the Troy & Bennington was its 5.25-mile branch from Hoosick Junction northeast to the state line; and the Western Vermont carried that branch the last two miles on into North Bennington, where it met its own Bennington-Rutland main line. Geometry is real right-of-way traced from OpenStreetMap, not a waypoint approximation: the Troy-Eagle Bridge half follows the abandoned alignment OSM labels 'Troy & Boston RR (Troy & Rutland)' (the Troy & Rutland Railroad shared this track from Troy to Eagle Bridge), the Eagle Bridge-Hoosick Falls-state line half follows the abandoned 'old B&M alignment', and the branch follows the still-active Vermont Railway Hoosick Branch. Two gaps in the OSM abandoned right-of-way north of Troy (about 4.7 km and 1.5 km, where the roadbed has been built over) are bridged with straight lines. Both ends are clipped to the real NY/VT boundary geometry from OSM. Era boundaries follow real, sourced corporate and service milestones; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not real timetables.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_and_Boston_Railroad (chartered April 4 1848, organized November 22 1849; completed Troy to the Vermont state line, 35 miles, in 1852; formed with the Hudson River Railroad the most direct line from New York to Montreal; consolidated into the Fitchburg Railroad in 1887, which the Boston and Maine leased in 1900)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Trains/ICC_valuations/Troy_and_Bennington_Railroad (incorporated May 27 1851 under the general laws of New York for 50 years, charter extended May 3 1901; single track from Hoosick Junction to the New York-Vermont state line, 5.249 miles, plus 1.047 miles of yard track; opened for operation under lease August 1 1852; perpetual lease dated August 1 1877; operated by the Fitchburg Railroad as lessee since June 30 1900 at $15,400 a year plus taxes; offices in Troy)

https://www.rutlandrailroad.org/history/timeline/ (Western Vermont Railroad incorporated November 5 1845; leased to the Troy & Boston November 1 1857; first Bennington & Rutland Railroad Company formed from the Western Vermont August 1 1865)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Bennington_station (Bennington and Rutland opened between its namesake cities, with a branch from North Bennington to White Creek on the New York border opening at the same time and connecting to the Troy and Boston; branch later operated by the Fitchburg and then the Boston and Maine, interchanging at North Bennington; B&R merged into the Rutland Railroad in 1867; Lebanon Springs Railroad built 1869 south from Bennington to Chatham NY, acquired by the Rutland in 1899; Second Empire station built 1880; Bennington-North Bennington passenger service ended in the early 1930s, replaced by buses; Green Mountain Flyer and Mount Royal served North Bennington until 1953; Vermont Railway resumed freight in 1964)

https://bennington.pastperfectonline.com/bysearchterm?keyword=Western+Vermont+Railroad (Bennington Museum: Western Vermont Railroad completed 1852 between North Bennington and Rutland, later became the Bennington & Rutland Railroad)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_Man (Boston & Maine's Minute Man, Boston North Station to Troy via Fitchburg, Greenfield, North Adams and Williamstown, debuted May 15 1926 and ran until January 18 1958; B&M cut intercity service back west of Williamstown later that year)

http://www.roadandrailpictures.com/forbmhoo.htm and https://penneyvanderbilt.wordpress.com/2014/06/28/hoosac-tunnel-to-troy-ny/ (station order and mileages west from North Adams: Williamstown 5, Pownal 9, North Pownal 12, Hoosick 18, Hoosick Falls 22, Eagle Bridge 26, Buskirk 28, Johnsonville 33, Valley Falls 36; rails between Hoosick Falls and Troy lifted around 1973)

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Frequency for every era is estimated. The end date of Boston & Maine passenger service specifically over the Troy & Bennington branch between Hoosick Junction and North Bennington is not sourced - the 1953 end date shown here is the documented end of passenger service at North Bennington (the Rutland's Green Mountain Flyer and Mount Royal), which may be later than the last B&M train off the branch. Exact opening date of the Western Vermont's state line-North Bennington section within 1852-53 is not pinned down; the Bennington Museum gives 1852 for completion, the North Bennington station article gives 1853 for the Bennington-Rutland opening.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Troy and Boston: Troy – Vermont State Line
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Chartered April 4 1848 and organized November 22 1849, the Troy & Boston completed its 35 miles from Troy to the Vermont state line in 1852, running up the Hudson through Lansingburgh and Melrose, then east up the Hoosic River through Schaghticoke, Valley Falls, Johnsonville, Buskirk, Eagle Bridge, Hoosick Falls and Hoosick Junction. The Troy & Rutland Railroad shared its track from Troy as far as Eagle Bridge. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Troy & Boston leased the Western Vermont Railroad on November 1 1857, taking control of the Vermont end of its own Bennington branch. With the Hudson River Railroad it formed what was billed as the most direct line from New York to Montreal. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: The Hoosac Tunnel opened to traffic in 1875 after nearly a quarter century of drilling, and this line became the western end of the Hoosac Tunnel Route: from the state line the trains continued over the Troy & Greenfield through the tunnel to North Adams, where they met the Fitchburg Railroad for Boston. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Troy & Boston was consolidated into the Fitchburg Railroad in 1887, ending its 39 years as an independent company and putting Troy and Boston under a single management for the first time. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: The Boston and Maine leased the Fitchburg in 1900, absorbing this line into the largest railroad system in northern New England. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The B&M's Minute Man, Boston North Station to Troy via Fitchburg, Greenfield, the Hoosac Tunnel, North Adams and Williamstown, debuted May 15 1926 and made this the route's best-known train. It last ran January 18 1958; the B&M cut intercity service back west of Williamstown later that year and the tunnel route went freight-only. The rails between Hoosick Falls and Troy were lifted around 1973, and that stretch is an abandoned right-of-way today. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Incorporated May 27 1851 under the general laws of New York, the Troy & Bennington was 5.249 miles of single track and nothing else - Hoosick Junction on the Troy & Boston northeast to the New York-Vermont state line - opened for operation under lease August 1 1852. It never ran itself: it existed to hand Bennington traffic to the Troy & Boston. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: Incorporated November 5 1845, the Western Vermont built its main line south from Rutland through Manchester to North Bennington and completed it in 1852; this short western branch carried it the last two miles from North Bennington to the New York state line, where it met the Troy & Bennington and so the Troy & Boston. Only the branch is drawn here - the Rutland-Manchester-North Bennington main line is not yet in this dataset. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
